guides.title: Exporting to Brazil — A Practical Manual for EU Businesses
guides.text:
EXPORTING TO BRAZIL 
A Practical Manual for EU Businesses 
Market entry, tariffs, customs, regulation and the EU–Mercosur Agreement 
Compiled from official sources: ICE – Italian Trade Agency and Confindustria 
Integrated and expanded edition – Business Matching Global (BMG) 
Reference date: July 2026 
A Business Matching Global publication 
© 2026 Business Matching Global. Reproduction, in whole or in part, is authorised only with attribution to the source. 
 

About This Manual 
This manual sets out to be a complete and authoritative source on exporting to Brazil under the new 
EU–Mercosur framework. We say this knowing that, despite every effort, no document on Brazil can 
ever be 100% complete: the subject is too wide, and the ground moves too fast. 
What follows reflects the state of the art as of 16 July 2026 — the tariff schedules, the customs 
guidance, the tax-reform transition rules and the regulatory requirements in force at that date. Some 
of these will have changed by the time you read this, oc casionally without warning. Rules are 
reinterpreted, deadlines shift, transitional regimes are extended or cut short. 
This is not a flaw of the manual; it is a feature of the market. Regulatory volatility is itself a component 
of Custo Brasil — as real a cost as freight or port storage — and pricing it in is part of doing business 
here. The companies that succeed in Brazi l are not those that found a perfect guide, but those that 
built a reflex of verifying before acting. 
Our advice, therefore, is simple: use this manual to understand the terrain, and before committing to 
any specific operation, check the current state of play with us. We monitor these changes daily from 
Belo Horizonte. Write to us at info@businessmatching.global — it is always the right first step. 
 
1. Why Brazil 
Brazil is the largest economy in Latin America and a natural gateway to the region. Key figures (2024–
2025):

Territory 8.5 million km² — 48% of South America

Brazil is also a global production powerhouse: the world's No. 1 producer of coffee, soybeans, 
sugarcane and orange juice; No. 2 in beef, poultry, pulp, biofuels and iron ore; No. 3 in milk, maize, 
fruit, tobacco and cotton; and the 8th largest oil produce r. This scale creates strong demand for 
machinery, technology transfer, specialized know-how and industrial equipment — precisely the areas 
where Italian and EU manufacturers are strongest.

2.2 EU–Brazil bilateral trade (2025) — Italy as a case study 
At bloc level, EU –Mercosur goods trade is large and remarkably balanced: in 2024 the EU exported 
roughly EUR 55 billion of goods to Mercosur against about EUR 56 billion of imports. In services the 
EU runs a clear surplus (around EUR 29 billion sold vs EUR 13 billion bought in 2023), and Brazil alone 
concentrates over 70% of these flows. The EU is also Mercosur’s largest foreign investor, with an FDI 
stock of some EUR 384 billion. The granular figures below use Italy — the manual’s primary statistical 
source — as an illustrative member- state case: the pattern they show (machinery -led EU exports, 
commodity-led imports, concentration in the South-Southeast) mirrors the profile of German, French 
and Spanish trade with Brazil as well. 
Flow Value Change vs 2024 
Italy → Brazil (exports) USD 7.1 bn +10.5% 
Brazil → Italy (exports) USD 5.4 bn +20.4%

Early-2026 signal (January–May): Brazil’s total exports reached USD 148.6 billion (+8.7%) and imports 
USD 115.9 billion (+3.2%). On the bilateral axis, Italy → Brazil slowed to USD 2.9 billion (−2.9%) while 
Brazil → Italy accelerated to USD 2.5 billion (+1 2.4%), cutting Italy’s surplus to USD 367.9 million 
(−49.6%). The window opened by the Agreement rewards early movers — competitors are already 
moving. 
 
What Brazil buys from Italy (by product share): machinery and mechanical equipment 33.5%, 
pharmaceuticals 12.1%, motor vehicles and parts 8.2%, electrical machinery 6.2%, iron/steel articles 
3.6%, optical/photographic/medical instruments 3.6%, plastics 3.5%. 
What Italy buys from Brazil: coffee (beans and roasted) 24.9%, paper and pulp 14.9%, mineral fuels 
and oils 14.5%, meat 6.3%, oilseeds (soy) 4.7%, animal feed 3.8%, iron ore 3.8%. 
Geographically, imports from Italy concentrate in São Paulo (38.9%), Minas Gerais (14.3%), Santa 
Catarina (9.7%) and Rio de Janeiro (9.5%) — together over 70% of the total. In value terms, machinery 
dominates in nearly every state, followed by pharmaceutic als and motor vehicles. At state level, the 
Italian product mix differs: in São Paulo, mechanical machinery leads (33.4%) followed by 
pharmaceuticals (13.7%); in Minas Gerais — the second-largest destination — machinery (27.7%) is 
followed by motor vehicle s (21.6%), pharmaceuticals (12.5%) and electrical equipment (12.4%); in 
Pernambuco, machinery alone accounts for 48.1% of Italian imports. 
Italian corporate presence in Brazil (2022–2025): FDI stock of EUR 10.9 billion, EUR 786 million inflow, 
and 1,104 Italian companies, 29% of them in the machinery and components sector. 86% of these 
companies are located in the South and Southeast of the country. 
3. Sector Opportunities for EU Companies 
• Steel and mining: Brazil is the world's 2nd iron ore exporter → demand for machinery for the 
steel industry. 
• Agriculture 4.0: Brazil is the world's No. 1 exporter of agricultural commodities → demand for 
custom software, big data analytics, agricultural drones, AI-managed animal feeding, blockchain 
traceability, smart irrigation. 
• Pharma and healthcare: Brazil is the world's 6th largest pharmaceutical market → machinery for 
innovative production/processing, including packaging. 
• Other high -potential sectors: food & beverage, automotive components, machine tools for 
marble/ceramics/glass/plastics/paper, waste treatment, cybersecurity, wellness. 
• Sanitation services: targeted by large government financing — Growth Acceleration Programme 
(USD 228 bn) and Nova Indústria Brasil (USD 52.6 bn). 
• Energy transition and ESG -driven demand: Brazil already runs one of the cleanest electricity 
matrices among large economies and is scaling wind, solar, biofuels/SAF and green -hydrogen 
projects — pulling in demand for EU components, EPC know -how, grid techn ology and 
certification services, while ESG requirements from Brazilian corporates and financiers open 
space for European sustainability expertise. 
4. The EU–Mercosur Agreement: What Changes 
The EU–Mercosur Interim Trade Agreement (Interim Trade Agreement, or 'iTA') entered into force on 
1 May 2026, covering the trade -only provisions of the wider EU –Mercosur Partnership Agreement 
(EMPA), which still requires ratification by EU member state parliaments for full entry into force. The 
iTA is the operative legal basis for preferential access today. 
The economic logic: Mercosur's Common External Tariff (MFN duties) ranges roughly 15–35%, 
historically far higher than the EU's average tariff — particularly on industrial goods and 
beverages. The EU secures the reduction of these high duties on its industrial and quality agri-
food exports, in exchange for gradually opening EU market access while keeping 
protections/quotas on sensitive agricultural products. 
Headline scope: progressive elimination of duties on 91% of EU exports to Mercosur and 92% of 
Mercosur exports to the EU, phased in over periods ranging from immediate (entry into force) to up 
to 15–18 years for the most sensitive lines (e.g. passenger cars, some auto parts). 
4.1 Tariff phase-out: how it works 
Each customs code in the agreement is assigned a 'staging category' — the number of years needed 
for full liberalization. Reduction begins at entry into force (Year 0) and proceeds in equal annual steps 
until the duty reaches zero. Common categories: 0 (im mediate), 4, 7, 8, 10 and 15 years. Some 
products carry special schedules with tariff- rate quotas (TRQs) — e.g. cars (15 years, transitional 
quota), EVs (18 years), beef, poultry, ethanol, sugar, rice. 
Reductions are calculated on whichever is lower: the 'base rate' negotiated in the agreement, or the 
MFN duty actually in force at the time — this protects the preference margin if a party later lowers its 
MFN tariff. 
Beyond the standard schedules, several agri-food lines follow special mechanisms: butter enters with 
an immediate 30% duty cut, yogurt with a 50% cut within 4 years, bananas at a fixed €75/tonne, and 
various fresh fruits and vegetables lose the ad valorem duty (immediately or over 7 –10 years) while 
the specific duty remains in force (“EP” categories). Cocoa preparations, chocolate and tomato 
preparations liberalise only within defined quotas.

The EU keeps ordinary trade-defence tools (anti-dumping, countervailing duties, global

Geographical Indications (about 57 Italian), a EUR 6.3 billion crisis fund for EU farmers, and 
mandatory compliance with EU sanitary/phytosanitary (SPS) standards on imports. One caveat 
for EU agri-food exporters: prior-user clauses allow existing Brazilian producers to keep 
marketing 'tipo parmesão' or 'gorgonzola'-style denominations already in use. In return, 37

4.3 The Brazilian perspective: Mercosur's liberalisation schedule in numbers 
Analysis by Brazil's industry confederation (CNI) crosses the dismantling baskets with actual Brazilian 
imports from the EU in 2024 — the clearest answer to the question every EU exporter asks: when does 
my sector become competitive in Brazil?

Reading the table: the immediate wins are real but limited — about one seventh of the trade value, 
concentrated in machinery (17.0% of the year -0 basket), food products (15.4%) and IT/electronics 
(13.2%). The centre of gravity is the 10 -year basket, which alone covers 41.8% of Brazilian imports 
from the EU, dominated by chemicals (30.1%) and machinery (15.0%). Over 90% of manufacturing 
lines follow linear schedules, and roughly 60% take 8 –15 years to reach zero — a deliberate cushion 
for Brazilian industry, and a planning horizon for EU pricing strategies. Source: CNI, Manual do Acordo 
de Parceria Mercosul-União Europeia, 2026. 
• Automotive carve -outs on the Mercosur side go beyond the headline schedules: electric and 
hybrid vehicles reach zero duty in 18 years, hydrogen vehicles in 25, 'new technologies' in 30; 
specific cars/tractors ('15V' category) liberalise over 15 years with an annual 50,000 -unit quota 
at reduced duty until year 8. 
• Agri-food quotas offered by Mercosur to the EU — directly relevant to Italian exporters: cheese 
30,000 t, milk powder 10,000 t, infant formula 5,000 t (each phased over 10 years) and garlic 
15,000 t (7 years), all with in-quota duties falling progressively to zero. 
The mirror image on the EU side: the EU offer covers over 99% of the tariff universe, and 82.7% of 
2024 Brazilian exports to the EU (USD 40.1 bn) enter duty-free immediately at entry into force — for 
industrial goods, over half of all lines are zero at year 0. Competitive pressure on the EU market from 
Mercosur suppliers therefore arrives faster than EU preferences materialise in Brazil. 
Three further disciplines from the goods chapter worth knowing: (i) a dedicated wine and spirits annex provides 
mutual recognition of oenological practices, labelling terms and certification based on OIV standards — a 
structural simplification for Italian wine exporters; (ii) Brazil reserved the right to impose export restrictions on 
critical minerals (the rate applied to the EU must be lower than to other destinations); (iii) Brazil retains 
import/export monopolies in petroleum, gas, hydrocarbons and nucle ar minerals. Source: CNI, 2026. 
5. Rules of Origin — the Core of Preferential Access 
Getting the tariff cut is not automatic: the importer must claim it and prove the goods are 'originating' 
under the agreement's rules. A product qualifies as originating if it is: (a) wholly obtained in the EU or 
Mercosur; (b) made exclusively from originating materials; or (c) manufactured using non-originating 
materials that meet the Product Specific Rules (PSR) set out in Annex 3-B. 
5.1 The three PSR mechanisms 
• Change of Tariff Classification (CC / CTH / CTSH) — non-originating materials must fall under a 
different HS chapter/heading/sub-heading than the finished product. 
• MaxNOM (maximum value of non -originating materials) — non-originating inputs may not 
exceed a set percentage (commonly 40–50%) of the ex-works (EXW) price. 
• Specific processing rules — e.g. 'chemical reaction' for chemicals, 'double transformation' 
(yarn→fabric→garment) for textiles. 
A general tolerance allows up to 10% of the EXW price in non -originating materials even where the 
specific PSR is not fully met (lower thresholds apply in textiles). 
5.2 Bilateral cumulation 
Materials originating in the EU used in Mercosur manufacturing (and vice versa) can be treated as 
originating in the receiving party, provided the processing performed goes beyond the 'insufficient 
operations' listed in Art. 3.6 of the Agreement (packaging, labelling, simple assembly, sorting, cleaning, 
etc. do not qualify). Only bilateral cumulation is available — there is no diagonal cumulation with other 
trade partners.

Always verify the exact rule for your product's HS code in Annex 3-B — do not extrapolate from 
other trade agreements. Use the EU's My Trade Assistant / Access2Markets ROSA tool for a 
product- and route-specific check (see Section 17). 
6. Proving Origin 
The default proof is the 'Statement on Origin', a self-declaration by the exporter placed on an invoice 
or other commercial document. EU exporters must use the REX (Registered Exporter System) and 
quote their REX number; registration is mandatory above EUR 6,000 per consignment. Mercosur 
exporters may, during a transitional period of up to 5 years, alternatively use certificates of origin 
issued by authorised bodies. 
Formal requirements matter. The statement must reproduce the standard wording of Annex 3 -C on 
the invoice or another commercial document that clearly identifies the goods, and the origin must be 
declared generically as “European Union” (or “EU”) or “Mercos ur” — never the individual member 
state, and never both blocs on the same statement. EU statements under REX need no handwritten 
signature; Mercosur exporters using self-certification must quote their national tax ID (CNPJ for Brazil, 
CUIT for Argentina, RUT for Uruguay) and sign, whether by hand or electronically. 
Customs must tolerate obvious clerical slips (typos in names, addresses or descriptions) that raise no 
doubt about the match between document and goods. Two defects, however, are treated as blocking: 
a wrong exporter reference number (REX, CNPJ, CUIT, RUT) and a product description too vague to 
verify tariff eligibility — either leads to outright denial of the preference. No proof of origin is required 
for occasional, non -commercial shipments below EUR 500 (private consignments) or EUR 1,200 
(travellers’ personal luggage) on the EU side. 
1. The statement is valid for 12 months from issuance. 
2. Exporters and importers must keep the statement and supporting documents for at least 3 years. 
3. A statement can be issued retroactively, within 2 years of importation. 
4. Customs authorities may verify origin post -clearance; the exporting party's authority must 
respond within 10 months, or preference is denied and duties (plus interest/penalties) are 
recovered. During the verification the importer can normally obtain release of the goods against 
a financial guarantee covering the full MFN duty. Note that the importing customs authority 
cannot approach the foreign exporter directly or inspect its premises: every request runs through 
the customs authority of the exporting country, which alone examines the exporter’s records and 
reports back. 
A significant regulatory update — EU Implementing Regulation 2026/1183 (in force 23 June 
2026) — strengthens REX-based self-certification, standardises supplier's declarations (new 
Annex 22-15 dataset) and introduces an electronic proof-of-origin system (e-PoC EU). General 
rules apply from 23 December 2027; supplier's-declaration rules from 23 June 2028. Companies 
should use the transition period to review supplier declarations, formalise REX governance, and 
prepare documentation systems now. 
6.1 Triangular operations and the non-alteration principle 
Originating goods that transit through third countries must remain unaltered and under customs 
control: only preservation and logistics operations are allowed. If goods are cleared through customs 
in an intermediate country — even temporarily — the preference can be lost. Keep continuous transit 
documentation (cargo manifests, transit declarations, proof of non-manipulation) for the whole route. 
When an EU trader buys from a Mercosur producer and resells without transformation (or vice versa), 
replacement statements of origin allow the intermediary to issue a new attestation based on the one 
received from the original supplier, provided the goods are not substantially modified. Note the 
asymmetry with Paraguay, which in the initial phase operates only with traditional certificates of origin 
issued by authorised bodies — different document flows, times and costs than the self -certification 
used by Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay (via CNPJ, CUIT or RUT identifiers). 
Tax angle: because import VAT is calculated on the customs value plus duty, every duty reduction under the 
Agreement also shrinks the VAT-at-import base — a direct cash-flow benefit for the importer. Triangular 
structures involving related parties should additionally be screened for transfer -pricing and permanent-
establishment exposure. 
6.2 Duty drawback is allowed 
The Agreement does not prohibit the refund or suspension of duties on non-originating materials used 
to produce goods exported with preference. An EU manufacturer importing components from Asia 
under inward processing, assembling them into finished goods a nd exporting to Mercosur with the 
preferential origin can therefore recover the EU duties paid on those components — a material 
reduction in total supply-chain cost that many older EU agreements do not permit. 
6.3 Goods already in transit on 1 May 2026 — act by 1 November 2026 
The Agreement contains a transitional clause for goods that were in transit or in temporary storage 
when the iTA started to apply. Such goods can still claim the preferential rate, provided the proof of 
origin is presented to customs within six months of e ntry into force — i.e. by 1 November 2026. A 
consignment shipped from Brazil in March 2026 and declared for free circulation in the EU on 1 July 
2026 qualifies; the same consignment declared on 1 December 2026 does not. Importers with long 
ocean lead times should audit open shipments now. 
7. Customs Duties and Other Import Costs in Brazil 
7.1 The tax stack at the border 
Tax Description 
Dazio / Imposto de Importação Import duty 
IPI Tax on industrialised products 
ICMS State-level tax on circulation of goods/services 
AFRMM Merchant Marine surcharge 
PIS/PASEP and COFINS Federal social contributions 
 
Brazil is implementing a broad tax reform that will gradually unify these levies into a two-tier 
VAT: a federal CBS (Contribuição sobre Bens e Serviços) and a state/municipal IBS (Imposto sobre 
Bens e Serviços), fully in force by 2033. The practical challenge is the transition (2026–2032): test 
rates for CBS/IBS started in 2026, and importers will face the old taxes (ICMS, IPI, PIS/COFINS) 
and the new ones charged concurrently, with the old rates being phased down as the new ones 
ramp up. Landed-cost simulations are therefore only valid for the year they are run. Long-term 
supply, distribution and pricing contracts should include an economic-rebalancing clause 
(reequilíbrio econômico-financeiro) that reallocates the effect of tax-burden shifts during the 
phase-in — otherwise one party silently absorbs every change. 
Duties/taxes can be simulated using Brazil's official calculator (Receita Federal): 
http://www4.receita.fazenda.gov.br/simulador/BuscaNCM.jsp — you will need the NCM code (the 
Mercosur 8-digit tariff classification; the last 2 digits are Mercosur-specific). 
Do not rely on a generic correlation between the EU HS code and the Brazilian NCM: the first six digits 
coincide, but the 8 -digit NCM drives duty rate, staging category under the Agreement, licensing 
requirements and tax treatment. A misclassification on the import declaration triggers Receita Federal 
fines and can retroactively disqualify the Mercosur preference. Before the first shipment, have the 
classification validated against detailed technical sheets and drawings — and for borderline products, 
file a formal classification ruling request (Solução de Consulta) with the Receita Federal, which is 
binding on the authority. 
7.2 Additional import costs (approx. 5–10% of total import operation cost) 
• Freight forwarder fees 
• De-consolidation of shipment/goods 
• Warehousing 
• Union/labour dues at ports 
• Customs clearance fees 
• Inland transport to the importer 
• Prior import licences via SISCOMEX 
 
7.3 The import declaration: DUIMP and the Portal Único Siscomex 
Brazil has been migrating from the legacy Import Declaration (DI) to the DUIMP (Declaração Única de 
Importação) within the Portal Único Siscomex — a single -window redesign of the whole import 
process. The operational gains are concrete: licensing and regulatory permits are centralised in a single 
module (LPCO), cargo and declaration data are submitted once and reused across agencies, and the 
declaration can be registered before the vessel arrives. This pre -arrival processing (“desembaraço 
sobre águas”) allows low-risk cargo to be cleared while still at sea, cutting port storage — one of the 
most expensive and least predictable components of Custo Brasil — often from weeks to days. 
Practical implication for the EU exporter: confirm early which regime applies to your product flow 
and whether your importer of record (or conta e ordem trading company) is already operating under 
DUIMP, has the LPCO licences mapped, and transmits data pre-arrival. An importer still working on 
legacy processes hands back part of the tariff saving in storage and demurrage. 
8. Custo Brasil: Budgeting for the Real Cost of Doing Business 
Tariffs and border taxes are only the visible layer. Brazil imposes a structural cost premium on 
economic activity — known locally as 'Custo Brasil' — which official estimates have put at roughly one 
fifth of GDP per year. For a European exporter, ignoring it is the single most common cause of failed 
business plans: prices, margins and timelines built on EU cost logic systematically underestimate what 
it takes to land, sell and service a product in Brazil. 
Component What it means in practice 
Tax complexity Dozens of federal, state and municipal levies with distinct bases and credit 
regimes; tax compliance famously absorbs on the order of 1,500 hours/year 
for a mid-size company — the highest burden in the world. The 2026–2033 
VAT reform will simplify this, but both systems coexist during the transition. 
Logistics A road-dependent freight matrix (roughly two thirds of cargo), long inland 
distances, port congestion and high handling costs. Inland transport can rival 
ocean freight on some routes. 
Cost of capital Historically double-digit benchmark interest rates make local financing and 
buyer credit expensive; payment terms carry a real financial cost. 
Labour charges Social charges and benefits ('encargos') can nearly double the nominal salary 
cost of an employee; labour litigation is frequent and employee-friendly. 
Bureaucracy Licences, registrations and permits at three levels of government; processes 
are digitalising quickly but still require local expertise and patience. 
 
Practical rule: treat Custo Brasil as a design parameter, not a surprise. Build gross-up factors into 
pricing, add time buffers to every regulatory step, and validate the full landed-cost chain with a 
local partner before quoting. Companies that price Brazil like an EU market either lose money or 
lose the deal. 
One logistics lever deserves specific attention for destinations outside the São Paulo –South axis (the 
Northeast, the Centre- West, the North): road freight over thousands of kilometres can erode the 
entire tariff preference. Two alternatives are routinely underused by newcomers: cabotagem — 
domestic coastal shipping between Brazilian ports, increasingly competitive after the 2022 “BR do 
Mar” reform — and bonded inland terminals (portos secos / EADI), which move customs clearance 
close to the final market and defer import taxes until the goods actually leave the bonded warehouse, 
easing cash flow and cutting congestion-driven port costs. 
9. Market Entry Models: Who Imports, and on Whose Account 
Every import into Brazil requires a Brazilian importer of record: a local entity with a CNPJ (tax 
registration) and a valid 'RADAR' habilitation in the SISCOMEX foreign-trade system. RADAR is granted 
in tiers based on demonstrated financial capacity, and c aps how much a company may import per 
semester. A foreign exporter cannot clear goods in its own name — so the first strategic decision is 
who imports, and under which model. 
Model Key features 
Distributor / importer (own account) The Brazilian company buys, imports and resells at its own risk. Simplest 
for the exporter; least control over pricing, positioning and end-customer 
data. 
Importação por conta e ordem A licensed trading company imports on behalf and on the account of the 
real acquirer, handling customs, tax mechanics and logistics as a service. 
The commercial relationship and economics stay with the acquirer. 
Widely used by newcomers and for premium niche products, as it 
separates market development from customs execution. 
Importação por encomenda The trading company imports in its own name, but against a firm, pre-
agreed order from a predetermined buyer. Different tax treatment from 
conta e ordem — the distinction matters and is scrutinised by the Receita 
Federal. 
Commercial representative Governed by Law 4,886/1965, which grants strong statutory protections 
— including a termination indemnity of 1/12 of all commissions ever 
paid. Representation contracts must be drafted with Brazilian counsel; 
informal arrangements create the same liabilities. 
Local subsidiary Full control and eligibility for public tenders and local financing, but full 
exposure to Custo Brasil (labour, tax compliance, corporate obligations). 
Usually a second-stage move, once recurring volume justifies the fixed 
cost. 
 
The chosen model affects more than logistics: it determines who claims the Mercosur preference 
at customs, how ICMS and IPI cascade into the resale price, and who owns the customer 
relationship. Model selection should precede — not follow — partner search. 
A specific warning on commercial representation under Law 4,886/1965: because the statutory 1/12 
indemnity and the presumption of exclusivity operate by default, the contract must say expressly what 
the parties intend. Three clauses mitigate most disputes: (i) an explicit statement on exclusivity — 
granted or excluded, on both sides; (ii) a precise territorial delimitation, so the representative cannot 
claim commissions on indirect or online sales into other states; and (iii) measurable minimum 
performance targets contractually linked to termination for cause (rescisão motivada), which is the 
main lawful route to ending the relationship without the full indemnity. Draft these with Brazilian 
counsel before the first order — an exchange of e -mails can already constitute an informal 
representation relationship carrying the same liabilities. 
A channel increasingly asked about is direct e -commerce. Brazilian online retail is large and 
marketplace-dominated (Mercado Livre, Amazon Brasil, Magalu, Shopee), and it can be a low-cost way 
to test B2C demand. Be realistic about its limits: cross -border parcels are taxed under the Remessa 
Conforme regime (import duty plus state ICMS collected by the platform, with thresholds and rates 
that have changed repeatedly), which erodes price competitiveness on low- ticket items; and any 
serious volume still requires a local importer of record, nationalised stock and Portuguese -language 
after-sales. In practice, e-commerce works best as a complement to — not a substitute for — one of 
the import models above. 
10. Regulatory Approvals and Product Registration 
The tariff preference opens the border; sector regulators decide whether the product may actually be 
sold. Registration lead times of several months are normal — the regulatory track must start well 
before the commercial launch, and often before signing with a distributor (some registrations are held 
by the local importer, which affects switching costs later). 
Authority Scope 
ANVISA Health surveillance: pharmaceuticals, medical devices, cosmetics, sanitisers, and 
several food categories. Foreign plants may require inspection or certification; 
the local registration holder must be a Brazilian entity. 
MAPA Agriculture: products of animal and plant origin, beverages and wine 
(establishment registration plus product registration/labelling approval), animal 
feed, fertilisers. 
INMETRO Mandatory conformity assessment for a long list of industrial and consumer 
goods (electrical equipment, components, PPE, toys, pressure vessels and more). 
CE marking is not automatically accepted — testing or certification by accredited 
bodies may be required. 
ANATEL Any product with radio/telecom functionality, including Wi-Fi and Bluetooth 
modules embedded in machinery. 
IBAMA / Exército / PF Environmental controls on chemicals; army and federal police controls on 
specific restricted goods. 
 
Two cross-cutting requirements deserve special attention from EU manufacturers: 
• NR-12 (machinery safety): equipment placed on the Brazilian market must comply with Brazil's 
machine-safety norm. EU-conform machinery frequently needs adaptation (guards, commands, 
documentation in Portuguese), and conformity is typically attested by a Brazil- registered 
engineer (CREA) issuing the corresponding technical responsibility record (ART) — budget for this 
local step; CE files alone do not close it. Non -compliance exposes the local buyer to labour-
inspection liability — and is a recurring deal-breaker discovered too late. 
• Portuguese labelling: the Consumer Protection Code requires product information in Portuguese, 
with prescribed content varying by category. Labelling review is part of registration for food, 
beverages and cosmetics. 
 
10.1 What the Agreement changes: technical (TBT) and sanitary (SPS) commitments 
The Agreement does not remove Brazilian regulatory requirements, but it disciplines how they 
operate — several points directly reduce compliance friction for EU exporters: 
Conformity assessment: the EU keeps its supplier’s declaration of conformity system, Mercosur keeps 
third-party certification (INMETRO model) — but certificates issued by bodies of one Party can be 
accepted by the other, and both sides commit to internatio nal accreditation standards. Automotive 
annex: Mercosur recognises UNECE WP.29 regulations as the technical reference for its own rules and 
accepts test results based on UNECE requirements — reducing duplicate homologation for vehicles, 
parts and equipment. 
Labelling: mandatory marking rules must require only relevant information, without discrimination or 
delay; other languages and international symbols are admitted, and — crucially — labels may be 
corrected or completed at the point of import, with non -permanent/detachable labels and 
accompanying documents accepted where legitimate objectives allow (medicines excepted). This 
softens, without eliminating, the Portuguese-labelling burden described above. 
Transparency: new technical regulations affecting bilateral trade require a formal public consultation 
with a minimum 60-day comment window — EU companies (directly or via associations) can influence 
Brazilian rules before adoption. 
SPS / agri-food: for animals and products of animal origin the Agreement adopts a pre -listing system 
— the exporting Party submits a list of establishments complying with the importer’s sanitary rules, 
dispensing with prior individual plant inspections, wi thin defined deadlines and procedures. Border 
checks are simplified where the exporting authority’s guarantees and international standards (WOAH, 
IPPC, Codex Alimentarius) are met. For Italian cheese, cured meat and other animal-origin exporters, 
pre-listing is one of the Agreement’s most concrete operational gains. Source: CNI, 2026. 
11. Intellectual Property: Register Before You Enter 
Brazil is a first-to-file jurisdiction. Trademark rights belong to whoever files first with the INPI (national 
IP institute) — not to whoever used the brand first abroad. Filing the trademark (and the .com.br 
domain via Registro.br) before disclosing the b rand to prospective distributors or at trade fairs is 
inexpensive insurance against a well-known failure mode: finding one's own brand already registered 
by a former prospect. 
• Brazil has been a member of the Madrid Protocol since 2019, so international registrations can 
designate Brazil — but a local attorney remains advisable for oppositions and enforcement. 
• Paris Convention priority can backdate the Brazilian filing to the EU one — but only within 6 
months for trademarks and designs and 12 months for patents from the first EU filing. If a brand 
or invention is about to be shown at a Brazilian trade fair, chec k whether the priority window is 
still open and file before disclosure. 
• Patent examination has accelerated but remains slow by EU standards; Patent Prosecution 
Highway (PPH) routes can shorten timelines for qualifying applications. 
• NDAs with prospects should include express IP and non -registration clauses enforceable under 
Brazilian law, and distribution agreements should regulate the use and ownership of marks, 
domains and registrations held locally. 
Note the Agreement’s IP chapter perimeter: patent term extension and clinical test data exclusivity were 
excluded (TRIPS-level commitments remain) — relevant for pharma strategies; GI recognition procedures are 
expedited in both directions; and an IP Subcommittee plus border-measure provisions (customs enforcement 
against counterfeits) are established. Source: CNI, 2026. 
12. Payments, Currency and Counterparty Risk 
The Brazilian real is a volatile currency, and FX swings of 10 –20% within a year are not exceptional. 
Quoting in EUR or USD transfers the risk to the buyer — which is standard — but affects the buyer's 
resale economics and should be discussed openly; hedging clauses or price-review mechanisms keep 
relationships stable. Brazil's FX framework was modernised by Law 14,286/2021, but cross -border 
payments still flow through authorised FX banks with supporting documentation tied to the import 
declaration. 
For new relationships, secure instruments (advance payment, confirmed letters of credit, export credit 
insurance — e.g. SACE for Italian exporters) are the norm until a track record exists. Counterparty 
verification is unusually transparent in Brazil, and there is no excuse for skipping it: 
• CNPJ status and corporate data: free, real- time lookup on the Receita Federal website 
(registration status, activity codes, partners). 
• Certidões negativas: official clearance certificates for federal tax, social security and labour debts 
— routinely requested before signing. 
• Credit bureaus (Serasa Experian, Boa Vista) for payment behaviour, protests and score; judicial 
databases are public and searchable for litigation and recuperação judicial (court -supervised 
restructuring) filings. 
Retention-of-title clauses have practical limits in Brazil, and recovering goods from an insolvent 
buyer is slow. Exposure management — credit limits, insurance, staged deliveries — protects 
better than contractual clauses alone. 
The Agreement itself adds a layer of legal certainty here: the current transactions and capital movements 
chapter commits the Parties to free movement of capital linked to direct investment and guarantees 
repatriation of profits and invested capital, in freely convertible currency and in line with IMF principles. 
13. Services, Technical Assistance and After-Sales 
The trade agreement reduces duties on goods; it does not touch Brazil's taxation of cross -border 
services, which routinely surprises EU machinery and technology suppliers. Payments from Brazil for 
services, technical assistance, software licences and royalties attract a stack of withholdings and 
levies: 
Levy Typical incidence 
IRRF (withholding income tax) Generally 15% (25% for payees in listed low-tax jurisdictions) 
CIDE 10% on technical services, technology transfer and royalties 
Levy Typical incidence 
PIS/COFINS-Importação 9.25% on imported services 
ISS (municipal service tax) 2–5%, levied by the municipality of the Brazilian payer 
IOF-FX Financial transactions tax on the currency conversion 
 
Because Brazilian buyers usually expect a net price, the gross-up can push the effective burden to 40–
50% of the contract value. The Italy–Brazil double tax treaty mitigates some components but does not 
eliminate most withholdings. Practical consequences: 
• Separate goods and services contractually: bundling installation, training and software into the 
machine price or splitting them changes the total tax bill materially — model both before quoting. 
• Consider delivering training in the EU (customer travels) versus in Brazil; on -site technical work 
requires the appropriate temporary work authorisation for technicians — tourist entry for paid 
technical activity is a compliance risk. 
• After-sales is a decisive competitive factor for European capital goods in Brazil: plan spare -parts 
availability, response times and a local technical partner from day one. A cheaper competitor 
with local service regularly beats a better machine without it. 
What the Agreement does cover on services: commitments across the four GATS modes, including temporary 
entry and stay of key personnel, trainees, business sellers, contractual service suppliers and independent 
professionals — a legal basis relevant to sending technicians for installation and after -sales. Brazil adopted a 
positive-list approach (only listed sectors are covered; defence, health, education, mining and oil extraction are 
out), there is no dedicated investment chapter (establishment is covered only as ‘Mode 3’), and e- commerce 
commitments are minimal. Check whether your service sector is actually listed before assuming coverage. 
Source: CNI, 2026. 
14. Business Culture and Relationship Building 
Brazil is a relationship-first market. Decisions follow trust, and trust is built through repeated personal 
contact — trade fairs, visits, meals, follow-up — far more than through documentation quality. Cold 
outreach converts poorly; a warm introduction th rough a chamber, association or trusted 
intermediary changes response rates dramatically. 
• Language: Portuguese, not Spanish. Presenting in Portuguese — or at least providing materials in 
Portuguese — is noticed and reciprocated. Assuming Spanish works is a small but persistent 
irritant. 
• Tone and time: meetings are warm, personal and less rigidly scheduled than in northern Europe, 
but negotiation cycles are long. First meetings rarely close anything; they qualify you for the 
second one. Build calendar buffers and plan multiple trips. 
• Hierarchy matters: identify the actual decision -maker (often the owner in family -controlled 
companies, which dominate the mid-market) and match seniority in your delegation. 
• Regional differences are real: São Paulo is pragmatic and fast by Brazilian standards; Minas Gerais 
is relationship -driven and discreet ('mineiro' business culture values patience and trust); the 
South (Paraná, Santa Catarina, Rio Grande do Sul) is process -oriented with strong European 
heritage. 
• Continuity is the multiplier: markets forgive distance but punish absence. A consistent local 
presence — direct or through a trusted local orchestrator — compresses sales cycles more than 
any pricing lever. 
15. Partner Search and Qualification: A Structured Process 
Most Brazil failures are partner failures. The distributor met by chance at a fair, granted national 
exclusivity on enthusiasm, is the classic error. A disciplined sequence protects both sides: 
1. Market thesis first: define target segment, channel, price positioning and the entry model 
(Section 9) before contacting anyone. 
2. Long-list from verified sources: sector associations, chambers of commerce, fair catalogues, state 
investment agencies — not search engines alone. 
3. Screening: CNPJ and certidões check, financials where available, credit score, litigation search, 
reference calls with current suppliers (Section 12). 
4. Structured B2B meetings: a clear agenda, materials in Portuguese, and interpretation where 
needed; evaluate technical capacity, sales structure and after- sales resources on site, not from 
slides. 
5. Pilot transaction: a limited first order with defined KPIs before any framework agreement. 
6. Formalisation: contract under Brazilian counsel, IP protections in place (Section 11), and territory 
or exclusivity granted only against measurable performance commitments, with review clauses. 
Institutional allies reduce search costs and add credibility: ICE offices, the bilateral Italian 
chambers (ITALCAM São Paulo and the regional chambers, including Minas Gerais), sector 
associations and state agencies. Business Matching Global operates on this corridor as an 
orchestrator of exactly this sequence — from market thesis to pilot transaction — transferring 
the method to the exporter's own team rather than creating dependency. 
16. Public Procurement: A New Market — With Brazilian Characteristics 
For the first time, the Agreement gives EU suppliers non -discriminatory access to covered Brazilian 
federal tenders — a market previously closed to foreign bidders on equal terms. Coverage was 
renegotiated in the 2024 'Brasília Package' precisely to preserve Brazil's use of state purchasing power 
as industrial policy, so the opportunity must be read with realism: 
• Thresholds and phasing: coverage values for Brazilian central entities are higher until year 7 of 
the Agreement and fall from year 8 — the market opens gradually. Sub -central (state -level) 
coverage exists but varies state by state. 
• Exclusions: purchases by the public health system (SUS) and by food-security and school-feeding 
programmes are entirely outside the Agreement. 
• Offsets without time limits: contracting entities may require local content, technology transfer or 
R&D commitments from suppliers indefinitely. National preference margins for Brazilian goods 
and services are preserved, as are set -asides of up to 25% of a contract for Brazilian micro and 
small enterprises. 
• Only listed services are covered (positive -list approach); all goods are covered unless expressly 
excluded. 
Strategic reading: the permanent offset regime penalises pure product exporters but rewards 
suppliers able to offer technology transfer, local partnerships and know-how — exactly where 
European industry is strongest. On the EU side, Brazilian firms gain reciprocal access to central-
entity tenders above SDR 130,000 for goods and services (SDR 5,000,000 for construction). 
Source: CNI, 2026. 
17. Practical Tools

The Agreement’s SME chapter also obliges both sides to maintain public websites with agreement texts, tariffs, 
rules of origin and sanitary measures in SME-friendly form, searchable by tariff code (Mercosur must 
implement within 3 years of entry into force), with designated SME Coordinators on each side — worth 
monitoring as a free first-stop resource. 
18. Authorised Economic Operator (AEO) Status 
The Agreement (Art. 4.8) commits both sides to a partnership programme for trusted operators. AEO 
status (granted under EU Customs Code criteria: customs/tax compliance record, reliable record -
keeping, financial solvency, competence/qualification standards, security standards) brings faster 
clearance, fewer physical checks, simplified documentation and deferred duty payment. 
A key forward -looking element is Mutual Recognition (MRA) of AEO status between the EU and 
Mercosur countries, envisaged under Art. 4.2(2)(f) — once operational, EU-certified operators would 
benefit from reduced checks and priority clearance directly in Mercosur customs, and vice versa. 
 
18.1 Beyond AEO: trade-facilitation commitments you can invoke 
The customs chapter goes beyond the WTO Trade Facilitation Agreement on several points of daily 
operational value: binding advance rulings on tariff classification and origin must remain valid for at 
least 3 years (the WTO requires only a ‘reasonable’ period); a 48 -hour release target applies to low -
risk cargo under common risk-management criteria; and the Parties commit to electronic documents 
and signatures, single -window filing, interoperable systems, electronic payment acceptance and 
expedited clearance for perishables. 
Temporary admission is granted duty-free for an agreed list of goods with acceptance of ATA carnets 
— directly useful for demo machinery, trade -fair samples and professional equipment on the Brazil 
circuit (Section 21 fairs). 
Counterweight — the anti-fraud clause: in case of proven systematic failures or fraud in obtaining 
preferential treatment, or failures in origin obligations and mutual customs assistance, the injured 
Party may temporarily suspend the preferential treatment . Sloppy origin management is therefore 
not only a company-level risk (duty recovery, penalties) but can contribute to sector-level suspension. 
Source: CNI, 2026. 
19. Export Control — Don't Assume the Trade Deal Covers Everything 
A free trade agreement lowers tariffs; it does not lift export control obligations. EU Regulation 
2021/821 on dual-use items (goods, software or technology with both civil and military application) 
still requires case -by-case verification: product classification against Annex I, destination, end -user, 
and declared/foreseeable end-use — regardless of the Mercosur preference. 
General export authorisations (AGEU) offer simplified routes for certain operations 
(repair/replacement, temporary exports for trade fairs, specific software/technology) but their 
coverage differs by country: several AGEUs apply to Argentina and Brazil, while Paraguay and Uruguay 
more often require individual authorisation. As of writing, no EU sanctions regimes target Argentina, 
Brazil, Paraguay or Uruguay — but this is independent of, and does not replace, dual-use screening. 
20. Environmental and Sustainability Conditions 
20.1 Non-regression and sustainable trade 
The Agreement includes a 'non-regression clause' (Art. 18.2): parties may set their own environmental 
and labour policies but must not weaken protection levels to attract trade or investment. It also 
commits both sides to preventing deforestation and increasing forest cover from 2030, and to 
developing joint value chains in critical minerals, EV batteries, green hydrogen and sustainable 
biofuels. 
20.2 CBAM (Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism) 
The EU's carbon border levy applies to cement, iron, steel, aluminium, electricity, hydrogen and 
fertilisers. Its application generated friction, especially for fertilisers and steel; in January 2026 the 
Commission reduced import duties on key fertiliser inputs (ammonia, urea) and opened the way for 
temporary CBAM suspensions for that sector to unblock the agreement, alongside a EUR 45 billion 
support package for EU farmers from 2028. 
20.3 EUDR (Deforestation Regulation) 
The EUDR bars market access for commodities linked to deforestation after 31 December 2020, 
directly affecting Mercosur soy and cattle products, and requires due -diligence with 
geolocation/traceability data. Implementation has been postponed to end-2026 for large companies 
and mid-2027 for SMEs to allow adaptation. 
Combined, the Agreement, CBAM and EUDR create a 'conditional trade' model: preferential 
market access is increasingly tied to sustainability and traceability compliance, not tariffs alone. 
21. Support Available from the Italian Trade Agency (ICE) 
ICE is present in Brazil with an office in São Paulo and a trade promotion desk (PdC) in Rio de Janeiro, 
offering: participation in fairs, conferences and events; assistance with registration of animal- origin 
products; market studies, sector notes and anal ysis; and business partner search with B2B 
matchmaking. Contact: sanpaolo@ice.it. 
2026 collective Italian participations at Brazilian trade fairs include (selection): CIOSP (dental, Jan), 
Marmomac Brazil (stone, Feb), Expo Revestir (coverings, Mar), Feimec (machine tools, May), Wine 
South America (May), Apas Show (food/retail, May), Hos pitalar (medical, May), Fispal Food Service 
(May), Fispal Tec (packaging, Jun), Fenaf (foundry/metallurgy, Jul), Febratex (textile, Aug), Exposibram 
(mining, Aug), Seafood Show Latin America (Oct), plus Gamescom Latam (video games, Aprâ May), 
the SÃ£o Paulo Book Biennial (Sep) and Expocine (Sepâ Oct). Outbound missions cover energy 
transition, wine, fashion, eyewear, textile technology and agricultural machinery. 
Beyond promotion, check the financial toolbox before self- funding market entry: Italian companies 
can access SIMEST subsidised internationalisation loans (Law 394/81 funds — market-entry, trade 
fairs, digitalisation, e-commerce — periodically offered with a partial non-repayable component) and 
SACE export-credit insurance and guarantees; every other member state runs analogous instruments 
through its national export-credit agency and promotion network — a non-exhaustive map: Germany 
(federal “Hermes cover” export guarantees administered via Allianz Trade, plus KfW IPEX -Bank for 
export and project finance, and GTAI for promotion), France (Bpifrance Assurance Export for state 
guarantees and subsidised instruments, Business France for promotion), Spain (CESCE f or export 
credit insurance, COFIDES for internationalisation financing, ICEX for promotion), Portugal (COSEC and 
AICEP), the Netherlands (Atradius Dutch State Business), Belgium (Credendo), Austria (OeKB), 
Denmark (EIFO), Sweden (EKN with SEK funding), Finland (Finnvera) and Poland (KUKE with BGK). The 
instruments differ in detail but cover the same three needs — credit insurance, buyer/supplier 
financing and market-entry grants or soft loans. These instruments materially change the economics 
of the first two years in Brazil and are routinely left unused. 
22. Quick-Start Checklist for an EU Exporter 
1. Classify your product under the correct HS/CN code and find the matching NCM code for Brazil. 
2. Check the applicable staging category and current preferential duty in Annex 2-A (or via My Trade 
Assistant). 
3. Identify the Product Specific Rule for your HS code in Annex 3 -B and confirm your product 
qualifies (CTH / MaxNOM / specific process). 
4. Register as an exporter in REX if consignment value will exceed EUR 6,000. 
5. Prepare the Statement on Origin on the commercial invoice; retain supporting documentation 
(bill of materials, supplier declarations, cost breakdowns) for at least 3 years. 
6. Choose the entry model (distributor / conta e ordem / encomenda / representative / subsidiary) 
and verify your importer's CNPJ status and RADAR capacity. 
7. Map regulatory requirements early: ANVISA / MAPA / INMETRO / ANATEL registrations, NR -12 
compliance for machinery, and Portuguese labelling. 
8. File your trademark with the INPI (and register the .com.br domain) before disclosing the brand 
to prospects. 
9. Run counterparty due diligence (CNPJ, certidões negativas, credit score, litigation) and secure 
payment terms for the first transactions. 
10. Model the tax gross -up on any services, installation, training, software or royalty component 
(IRRF, CIDE, ISS, PIS/COFINS-Importação). 
11. Verify any dual-use classification (Annex I, Reg. 2021/821) and end -use/end-user due diligence, 
independent of the trade preference. 
12. Budget for Brazilian import taxes (Import Duty, IPI, ICMS, PIS/COFINS) and ancillary costs (5–10% 
of operation value) using the Receita Federal simulator — and for Custo Brasil in operating plans. 
13. Check EUDR/CBAM relevance if your product or its inputs touch agri -commodities or carbon -
intensive materials. 
14. If your sector sells to the public buyer, monitor Brazilian federal tenders now covered by the 
Agreement — minding SUS exclusions, offset requirements and national preference margins. 
15. Consider AEO status for faster, cheaper customs clearance and future mutual- recognition 
benefits. 
16. Plan after-sales (spare parts, technical partner, response times) before the first sale, not after. 
17. Use ICE São Paulo/Rio, the bilateral chambers and Access2Markets as first ports of call for market 
intelligence and structured partner search. 
Sources

in Italy', EU–Mercosur Webinar, 3 July 2026. 
Confindustria, 'Mercosur — Guida operativa all'Accordo UE –Mercosur per le imprese italiane', July 
2026 (with contributions from Studio Armella & Associati, Van Bael & Bellis, KPMG, Studio Padovan, 
Enrico Perticone Consulting, Studio Santacroce & Partners, and Easyfrontier). 
CNI – Confederação Nacional da Indústria, 'Manual do Acordo de Parceria Mercosul-União Europeia', 
Brasília, 2026 — Brazilian-side analysis used in Sections 4, 10.1, 11 –13, 16 and 18.1; reproduction 
permitted with attribution per the publication's terms. 
Sections 8 –15: elaborated by Business Matching Global from Brazilian primary sources (Receita 
Federal, ANVISA, MAPA, INMETRO, ANATEL, INPI, Law 4,886/1965, Law 14,286/2021, NR-12) and BMG 
field practice on the Italy–Brazil corridor. 
This manual is a summary for orientation purposes. Always verify current duties, staging categories, 
rules of origin and regulatory requirements against the official Agreement texts (Annexes 2-A and 3-
B), Access2Markets and the competent Brazilian authorities before relying on figures for a specific 
shipment.

guides.title: Brazil's Health Market — operational guide for pharma, devices and supply chain
guides.text:
Brazil's Health Market 
An operational guide for European pharmaceutical, device and supply-chain 
companies 
Edition 1.0 — July 2026 
#CustoBrasil | Notas do Corredor — ebook series 
 

How to read this guide 
This guide is written for one specific reader: the European company — manufacturer, licensor, 
machinery builder, ingredient supplier, distributor or investor — that has decided Brazil is worth 
a serious look, and now needs to know where the doors actually are. 
It is not a market report. Market reports describe demand. This guide describes architecture: who 
buys, under which rules, through which entity, at which price ceiling, and what the Brazilian state 
has decided to reward. In a regulated sector, architecture beats demand. A molecule that everyone 
wants is worth nothing until it has a registration holder, a price band, a distribution licence and a 
channel. 
Three warnings before you start. 
– Brazil is not one market. It is an archipelago of mini-markets — public and private, federal 
and state, retail and hospital, industrial and magistral — with different rules, different 
buyers and different economics. Part Two maps them. 
– The rules changed in 2026. Two of them, in the same quarter: the EU–Mercosur interim 
trade agreement entered into provisional application on 1 May 2026, and Law 15,471 of 20 
July 2026 rewrote the way the Brazilian state buys health products. Anything written before 
this year is, for practical purposes, out of date. 
– The tariff door and the procurement door are not the same door. This is the single most 
important sentence in this guide, and Part Five explains why. 
A solution on paper is not a corridor. Everything in this guide is public knowledge; 
what is scarce is the implementation. 
 
Part One — Why Brazil, and why now 
1.1 The size of the thing 
Brazil is among the ten largest pharmaceutical markets in the world and, in the last three years, 
one of the fastest growing of them. Pharmaceutical retail turnover passed R$ 240 billion in the 
twelve months to late 2025, growing at close to 11% year on ye ar, and the sector's own consensus 
for 2026 sits around 10 –12% growth. The industry association's forecasting forum has put 2025 
growth at 12.1% and 2026 at 10.6%. 
The physical channel is unusually dense. The country has more than 93,000 pharmacies and 
drugstores — roughly one for every 2,300 inhabitants, against one primary public health unit for 
every 4,400. Large chains hold a little under half of the store base; the rest is independents and 
associative networks. Online sales already account for close to 19% of the market and are still 
climbing. 
Underneath the numbers is a demographic engine that does not reverse. Brazil has some 24.7 
million people aged 65 or over today and is projected to have around 50 million by 2050 — a 
doubling of the highest-consumption cohort inside one investment horizon. 
1.2 A week in July, as an illustration 
On 29 July 2026 the Brazilian regulator, Anvisa, granted registration to five new semaglutide pens 
in a single decision, taking the country to six approved products with that molecule. Novo Nordisk's 
exclusivity had lapsed in March. The five approvals went to a Swiss company selling through a 
partnership with a Brazilian firm and a European laboratory; to an Indian manufacturer; to a 
subsidiary of that Indian manufacturer; and to two subsidiaries of a Brazilian group, one of them 
again in partnership with the same Indian manufacturer. 
Read that list again slowly, because it is the whole guide in miniature. Not one of the five is a 
European multinational selling directly into Brazil. Every single one is a combination: a molecule 
from one place, a registration holder in another, a manufac turing site in a third, a commercial 
channel in a fourth. The semaglutide market moved R$ 5.6 billion in Brazil last year; together with 
the competing molecule, analysts expect the segment to reach R$ 35 billion in the formal market 
by 2030. 
The product crossed the border. The company did not. That is the normal shape of a 
successful entry into Brazilian pharma — and it is a shape most European exporters are 
not organised for. 
Two further details from the same week are worth keeping. First, the regulator noted that 68% of 
all registration requests filed for injectable devices in obesity and diabetes are now for synthetic 
products — a structural shift away from biological routes, and a shift that changes which suppliers 
matter. Second, the next molecule in the pipeline, retatrutide, is expected to be filed for Brazilian 
registration only after United States approval, with the sponsor targeting the first quarter of 2027. 
Brazil is now close enough to the front of the queue that the lag is measured in quarters, not years. 
 
 
 
1.3 What the growth is actually made of 
Three engines, in descending order of certainty: 
– Chronic disease and ageing. Diabetes, hypertension, obesity and oncology drive both 
retail volume and the public budget. Metabolic products are the loudest current example, not 
the whole story. 
– Patent expiries. A dense calendar of expiries over the next five years is the main opening 
for generics, similars and synthetic alternatives — and, for European players, for licensing 
and contract manufacturing rather than direct sales. 
– Centralised public purchasing. The federal government is concentrating and expanding 
its buying power, and — as Part Four explains — has just given itself a statutory instrument 
for using that power as industrial policy. 
 
CURIOSITY — THE BORDER A PATENT DOES NOT CROSS 
An aside, offered as a curiosity rather than as advice, because it illustrates a principle that costs 
European companies real money: intellectual property is territorial, and so is the value of a registration. 
Semaglutide lost exclusivity in Brazil in March 2026, which is why six products with that molecule now 
exist there. The competing molecule, tirzepatide, remains under patent in Brazil until 2036 — so on the 
Brazilian side of the border it has one supplier and a box can cost upwards of R$ 3,400. 
On the Paraguayan side, several laboratories registered with the local sanitary authority, Dinavisa, 
produce tirzepatide pens under their own brand names. Where a patent was never filed, there is no 
patent to infringe: in their own jurisdiction those producers are doing something entirely lawful. What 
is unlawful is the next step — the pens are not registered with Anvisa, their import into Brazil has been 
barred since late 2025, and they nonetheless circulate through social networks and messaging apps at 
a fraction of the Brazilian price, promoted by influencers. A university toxicology centre analysed 
samples and did find tirzepatide in them; the regulator's answer was that the presence of the molecule 
is not the point, since an unregistered product cannot be traced or recalled. A patients' association has 
gone to court to challenge the ban. 
Two lessons for the European reader, both dull and both expensive. First, your patent map and your 
registration map are not the same map, and neither is continent-wide: Mercosur is a customs union, 
not a single regulatory or intellectual-property territory. Second, wherever a registered price and an 
unregistered substitute differ by a factor of three, an informal channel will appear — and it will erode 
your Brazilian volumes long before anyone tells you it exists. 
 
Part Two — One country, five markets 
The most expensive mistake a European company makes in Brazil is to build one strategy for "the 
Brazilian market". There are at least five, and they do not share buyers, margins, registration logic 
or timelines.

A few notes on the two that European companies systematically underestimate. 
The public market is not a customer. It is a policy instrument. 
The unified health system is the largest single buyer in the country, and since July 2026 the law 
says explicitly that its purchasing power is an instrument of industrial policy. You do not win it 
with a better price from a European plant. Part Four is about what you do win it with. 
The magistral market is a real industry, and it is European-friendly. 
Compounding pharmacies are not a folkloric leftover. The segment turned over R$ 13.2 billion in 
2025 and grew 29.3% in real terms between 2021 and 2025, against 21.2% for the economy as a 
whole. Around 8,700 establishments, roughly 80% of them small busine sses, and the fastest 
growth in the North and Northeast. They buy raw materials, excipients, packaging, small -scale 
equipment, quality-control instruments and formulation know-how — categories where European 
suppliers are competitive and where the regulatory barrier is a fraction of the one facing a finished 
medicine. 
If your product is an input rather than a dosage form, the compounding channel gives 
you a Brazilian revenue line while the registration of your finished product is still in the 
queue. 
 
Part Three — The regulator: what Anvisa actually requires 
3.1 The three things you cannot avoid 
Whatever your product, three requirements sit at the entrance and none of them can be outsourced 
to a freight forwarder. 
– A Brazilian legal entity holding the authorisation. Medicines and health products are 
registered to a company established in Brazil holding a valid operating authorisation (AFE) 
compatible with the activity. A foreign manufacturer does not hold a Brazilian registration 
directly; a Brazilian entity does — your subsidiary, your licensee, your distributor or your 
partner. Whoever holds it, controls the asset. 
– Good manufacturing practice certification of the manufacturing site. Your 
European plant must be certified — by Anvisa itself or, increasingly, through recognition of 
an equivalent foreign authority's inspection. 
– A price, before you sell. Prescription medicines are subject to price regulation by the 
CMED chamber. The ceiling is set before commercialisation, and it is not a formality: as Part 
Six shows, from 2027 it also determines your tax treatment. 
3.2 Registration categories, and why the label matters 
Brazilian law does not allow generics of biological products. This is why the wave of semaglutide 
approvals arrived as "new medicines" — synthetic alternatives to a biological product — rather than 
as generics. The category determines the dossier, the timeline, the price band and the substitution 
rules at the pharmacy counter. Classify your product wrongly at the start and you will spend two 
years correcting it. 
Statutory maximum analysis periods were fixed by Law 13,411/2016: broadly 365 days for a new 
medicine and 120–200 days for generics and similars, with shorter windows for lower-risk devices. 
Treat these as the legal ceiling, not the planning assumption; th e practical range for a complete, 
well-prepared dossier is usually eight to eighteen months depending on complexity. A simplified 
procedure introduced at the end of 2024 covers generics, similars, specific, dynamised, herbal and 
radiopharmaceutical products, and biologicals, for companies with a valid AFE. 
3.3 Reliance: the door Europeans should be using 
Since 2022 Anvisa has operated a regulatory reliance framework, allowing it to make use of 
assessments, inspections and decisions already carried out by recognised Equivalent Foreign 
Regulatory Authorities. The European Medicines Agency is among them. The general criteria came 
in with RDC 741/2022; the operational criteria for the optimised analysis procedure — covering 
registration and post-registration of medicines, biologicals and vaccines, and the active-ingredient 
dossier adequacy letter — sit in Normative Instruction 289/2024. 
Two developments matter for planning. In May 2026 the agency approved changes to that 
instruction, including an extension from six to eighteen months of the window for submitting 
changes already approved by an equivalent authority under the optimised proce dure — a 
significant relief for post -registration management of a European portfolio. And the agency's 
2026–2027 regulatory agenda foresees revisiting the reliance procedure for good-manufacturing-
practice certification itself. 
A realistic expectation: reliance shortens technical analysis and reduces the number of formal 
queries. It has not, so far, dissolved the queue — between 2024 and 2025 the agency received 218 
reliance-based registration requests, and its own assessment was that the effect on the total backlog 
was limited. Use it as an accelerator, not as a substitute for a Brazilian regulatory function. 
The European dossier is an asset in Brazil. It is not a passport. It shortens the analysis 
of an application that still has to be filed by a Brazilian entity, in Portuguese, against 
Brazilian requirements. 
 
Part Four — The law that changed the game: Ensceis (Law 
15,471/2026) 
On 20 July 2026 Brazil enacted the National Health Strategy for the Health Economic -Industrial 
Complex, published the following day and in force immediately. It amends both the public 
procurement law and the organic health law, and it converts what had bee n a decade of shifting 
programmes into permanent statutory instruments. If you read only one part of this guide, read 
this one — it is the framework inside which every public-sector opportunity in Brazilian health will 
be decided for the next decade. 
4.1 The three instruments 
– Productive Development Partnership (PDP). A cooperation instrument between 
public institutions, private entities and credentialed strategic health companies, awarded by 
selection process and formalised in a specific supply contract. Technology transfer is not 
decorative: the receiving entity must obtain full access to the technology, including the 
master cell bank for biotechnological products. There is a required degree of national 
verticalisation of the active ingredient and of critical technological components, subject to a 
technical and economic feasibility study. In exchange, the Ministry of Health commits to 
purchase according to an agreed demand plan — a market guarantee. Prices must decline 
over the life of the partnership, with an additional discount once the patent lapses. 
– Local Development and Innovation Programme (PDIL). Requires the participation 
of at least one scientific and technological institution or public health producer, in 
partnership with a strategic health company. Payment is by validated phase, with continuous 
monitoring and technical-financial audit. 
– Technological Orders (Etecs). Health-sector adaptation of the innovation-law 
commissioning mechanism, to be detailed by executive regulation. 
4.2 The Strategic Health Company (EES) — the status that changes everything 
The law creates a credentialing status. To be credentialed, a company must cumulatively 
demonstrate technical, operational, financial and regulatory capacity; an industrial facility in 
Brazil; a history of research and development investment; and the ability to sustain production. 
What the status buys: 
– Regulatory priority — accelerated handling of registrations, licences and authorisations 
before regulators, and priority in public calls related to research, development and 
production of strategic health products. 
– Access to development-bank credit lines on favourable terms. 
– Eligibility for the direct-award and exclusive-tender routes described below. 
– A margin of preference in tenders, available where the company's productive capacity covers 
at least 30% of the quantity being procured. 
The mirror image is a restriction: decredentialing can be triggered where national sovereignty or 
continuity of supply to the health system is at risk, a company may be required to remain 
credentialed for a fixed period, and corporate acts that breach the conditions before formal 
decredentialing can be void. In plain terms, credentialing is a commitment, and it interacts directly 
with any future sale or restructuring of the Brazilian entity. 
4.3 What the law does to tenders 
– Direct award without tender for strategic health products originating from partnerships and 
technological orders, and for products developed under the local innovation programme 
where incorporated into the health system at market-compatible prices. 
– Tenders reserved exclusively to credentialed strategic health companies — a market reserve 
in the literal sense. 
– Margin of preference for national products meeting Brazilian technical standards, under the 
conditions above. 
– Centralised purchasing of strategic health products, to be defined by executive act — larger 
lots, fewer decisions, higher stakes per decision. 
– Tender documents may require, alone or cumulatively, physical space maintained in Brazil 
for research, development and industrialisation, and a minimum percentage of national 
content. 
– Consortia and special-purpose vehicles are expressly admitted, provided they are constituted 
before contract signature. 
For a European company the message is unambiguous: the Brazilian state has decided 
to buy presence, not price. Whoever manufactures, transfers and employs locally wins; 
whoever quotes from Europe competes for what is left. 
Note also what is still missing. The infra-legal regulation has not yet been issued, edital templates 
and internal procedures are being rewritten, and public buyers are in an institutional adaptation 
period. That gap is the window: the technical criteria b eing drafted now will define who qualifies 
for the next decade, and they are being drafted with input from whoever is present and credible in 
Brasília today. 
 
Part Five — The trade layer: EU–Mercosur, and the door that 
stays shut 
5.1 What entered into force 
The interim trade agreement between Mercosur and the European Union has been provisionally 
applied since 1 May 2026. Goods are covered in Chapter 2 of that agreement, replicated in the 
wider partnership agreement, which requires ratification by member-state parliaments and is not 
yet in force. 
The Mercosur offer covers roughly 91% of goods originating in the European Union, in immediate 
or linear phase-out baskets over 4, 8, 10 or 15 years. Medicines and pharmaceutical products are 
among the most significant European exports to Brazil today, and they are also among the domestic 
sectors identified as facing increased competition — which tells you both that the tariff relief is real 
and that it will be watched. 
Three practical consequences: 
– The preference is not automatic. Capturing it requires correct tariff classification, the 
right phase-out schedule and compliance with the product-specific rule of origin. For devices 
and diagnostics — products assembling components, sensors and electronics from several 
jurisdictions — origin mapping is materially harder than for simple goods, and requires 
auditable documentation at each stage. 
– There are defences. Decree 12,866/2026 regulates bilateral safeguards, organising the 
responses available where preferential imports threaten serious injury to domestic 
production. 
– For medical devices, the technical-barriers chapter may be worth more than 
the tariff. Certification, labelling and cybersecurity requirements drive time, cost and 
operational risk; a structured technical dialogue anchored in international standards 
changes those more than a few percentage points of duty. 
5.2 The carve-out you must not miss 
The agreement contains a government procurement chapter. It also contains a carve-out excluding 
items destined for the public health system from that chapter's disciplines. In other words: the 
negotiated opening of Brazilian public procurement does not extend to the largest health buyer in 
the country. 
Put the two 2026 instruments side by side and the strategic picture resolves itself with unusual 
clarity.
