CHAPTER 4
Brazilian Culinary Context: Affinities
Brazilian cuisine is characterised by its openness to complex vegetable-based condiments. A
notable example is vinagrete, the classic accompaniment to churrasco, made with tomatoes,
onions, green peppers, white-wine vinegar and olive oil.
Ajvar positions itself as a qualitatively superior alternative to vinagrete, or as a complementary
option. While vinagrete is fresh, acidic and chunky, ajvar offers smoky, roasted notes and a dense,
spreadable consistency that local fresh condiments lack. The shared use of core ingredients such
as peppers, onions and garlic paves the way for acceptance of ajvar's flavour profile. This sensory
similarity lets ajvar transcend the perception of a niche ethnic product — and it should be
marketed as a gourmet upgrade of a traditional condiment.
In addition, ajvar's pronounced umami richness makes it an excellent accompaniment to
meat-based dishes. For consumers reducing their red-meat consumption, a robust, smoky
condiment like ajvar compensates for the absence of animal protein, delivering savoury
complexity even in plant-forward meals.

CHAPTER 5
Positioning: Naturally Vegan and Clean Label
Ajvar's market entry aligns with the exponential growth of the plant-based sector. In 2023 the
global plant-based meals market was valued at US$ 52.4 billion, with projected growth at a
compound annual rate (CAGR) of over 18.1% between 2024 and 2032.
When produced according to the authentic recipe — peppers, aubergines, oil and salt — ajvar
lends itself naturally to clean-label branding, answering consumer demand for healthier, less
processed food.
Nutritional benefits

Rich in antioxidants, with vitamin C levels higher than an orange and a high beta-carotene content.

Lycopene (the red pigment) acts as a powerful antioxidant.

Naturally vegan, gluten-free and low in carbohydrates.

Compatible with low-carb and ketogenic diets.

CHAPTER 6
Cultural 'Tropicalisation': The Narrative in Brazil
For ajvar to reach its full sales potential, the strategy must go beyond the 'ethnic specialty' niche.
The focus is the organic integration of the product into local culinary traditions, presenting it as an
essential item that elevates the already established consumption habits of the premium retail
audience.
Connection to origin: artisanal Minas cheeses
Ajvar establishes a perfect sensory dialogue with the cheeses that define the identity of Minas
Gerais. Its smoky depth and umami richness contrast elegantly with the lactic acidity of a Canastra
cheese or the intensity of a well-cured Salitre. Where traditional chilli jams focus on sugar, ajvar
brings complexity and balance — positioning itself as the definitive accompaniment for the Minas
cheese board.
The 'red gold' of gourmet churrasco
Ajvar is presented as the evolution of vinagrete and chimichurri. Its unctuous texture allows it to
be used directly on prime cuts (picanha, ancho), delivering a roasted-pepper note that recalls the
flavour of the embers. It is the ready-to-use 'red gold' that adds value to the average ticket of the
meat and parrilla segment.
Pairing with bar snacks: queijo coalho and dadinho de tapioca
Queijo coalho: ajvar is the ideal partner for grilled coalho cheese. The natural acidity of the
peppers cuts through the fat of the cheese, while the smoky touch of the Maillard reaction
harmonises with the char of the fire. Dadinho de tapioca: we propose replacing the ubiquitous
chilli jam with ajvar. It keeps the vibrant colour and familiarity, but elevates the snack to a higher
gastronomic level — less sweet and far more aromatic.
Strategic tip: innovation and education
Success for exclusive items at premium grocers depends on consumer education. As premium
retailers have historically done when introducing unfamiliar products — for example, distributing
recipes to teach customers how to prepare a new fish — we will do the same with ajvar. We will
not deliver only a jar; we will deliver the 'how to use it': printed pairing suggestions and training
for staff, ensuring the customer knows exactly how to make ajvar the star of their next dinner or
reception.

CHAPTER 7
Regulatory and Sanitary Framework
In Brazil, regulatory authority over food products is split by their nature. MAPA is responsible for
products of animal origin and beverages. ANVISA regulates most processed foods for direct human
consumption, including vegetable preserves.
As a purely vegetable preserve, ajvar benefits from exemption from mandatory health
registration, under RDC No. 843/2024 and IN No. 281/2024 (which replaced the former RDC
27/2010). In practice this removes the bureaucratic risks and technical bottlenecks that typically
delay exports at origin, eliminating the need for lengthy scientific assessments and ensuring a
simplified import process with immediate time-to-market. Instead of full registration, the
applicable requirement is a Communication of Start of Manufacture or Import — a significantly
simpler administrative procedure filed with the local Health Surveillance.
Conditions to maintain the exemption

The formulation must remain unchanged — animal-origin ingredients or functional claims invalidate
the exemption.

Full compliance with Brazilian labelling rules: Portuguese translation, ingredient list, allergen
declaration (RDC 727/2022) and nutritional table.

Front-of-pack warning symbols (RDC 429/2020) where applicable.
Border control: dual jurisdiction
Each shipment is subject to dual jurisdiction at the border. ANVISA controls the product,
documentation and labelling. MAPA/VIGIAGRO controls the logistics components — particularly the
pallets. Solid-wood pallets must comply with the international phytosanitary standard ISPM 15. For
sensitive shipments, plastic (PBR) or pressed-wood (INCO) pallets — exempt from ISPM 15
requirements — are recommended.

Tariff Classification and Pricing Strategy
Correct tariff classification is decisive for the success or failure of customs clearance. An incorrect
NCM can lead to substantial fines, delays in sanitary release and incorrect tax calculations.
Correct classification: NCM 2005.99.90
After a detailed analysis of the Explanatory Notes to the Harmonised System (NESH) and Brazilian
administrative case law, the most robust and defensible classification is under Chapter 20 —
specifically subheading NCM 2005.99.90 ('Other vegetables prepared or preserved, not frozen').

Minas Gerais: Import Corridor (TTS)
The Minas Gerais Import Corridor, regulated as a Sectoral Tax Treatment (TTS) under Law
6.763/75, is particularly relevant for operations targeting the state itself. The regime grants full
deferral of ICMS on import — i.e., zero ICMS at customs clearance — provided clearance occurs in
Minas territory. On subsequent sales, the importer benefits from a presumed ICMS credit resulting
in an effective tax burden of approximately 1.5% on sales. The regime also postpones ICMS-ST
collection to the moment goods leave, significantly easing cash flow. For a product like ajvar,
whose initial market is Belo Horizonte and its metropolitan region, this corridor offers the ideal
combination of fiscal advantage and logistics proximity. Dry ports in the state make clearance in
Minas feasible — an essential requirement for the benefit. Vegetable preserves such as ajvar are
not on the regime's 'negative list' of excluded products.
Rio de Janeiro: RioLog
RioLog is built around deferral of ICMS on import. Normally an importer would pay ~20% ICMS at
clearance (18% base + 2% FECP); under RioLog this is deferred to the sale, freeing significant
working capital. For internal sales in Rio, the regime reduces the taxable base, resulting in an
effective ICMS rate of ~13% (including FECP). Accredited importers may apply a reduced MVA for
ICMS-ST. Greater Rio, with over 12 million inhabitants, offers an immediate consumer market and
reduces last-mile costs.
Santa Catarina: TTD 409
TTD 409 (Law 17.763/2019) is one of Brazil's most aggressive regimes for importers. It offers
deferral of ICMS on import with a reduced anticipation of just 2.6% in the first 36 months, falling to
1% from the 37th month. On interstate sales, the effective tax burden can reach just 1.4% in the
second phase, thanks to the presumed credit. The regime requires a headquarters or branch in SC
and clearance at Santa Catarina ports or airports. It is particularly advantageous for national
distribution, but has a logistical disadvantage when supplying the Minas market directly (distance
and freight cost).

Espírito Santo: FUNDAP
FUNDAP (Fund for the Development of Port Activities), in force since 1970 and recently extended
to 2032, offers deferral of ICMS on import with subsequent financing by Bandes (the ES
development bank) of up to 8% of the ICMS collected, at 1% annual interest and terms of up to 25
years; contracts are auctioned monthly with discounts of up to 90%. It is a financial rather than
purely fiscal regime, which gives it greater legal robustness. It requires a headquarters in ES and
clearance at the state's ports — an interesting option for larger volumes and distribution across
the South-East as a whole.
Strategic consideration
For the initial ajvar operation focused on Minas Gerais, the MG Import Corridor offers the best
cost/benefit: zero ICMS on import, an effective ~1.5% burden on sale, and immediate proximity to
the target market. As the operation scales to national distribution, a complementary structure via
SC (TTD 409) or ES (FUNDAP) can be evaluated to optimise the tax burden on interstate
operations. Crucially, all these state regimes will be phased out by 2032 under the tax reform (EC
132/2023). The window to exploit these incentives is therefore limited — reinforcing the
first-mover argument.

CHAPTER 10
Impact of the Tax Reform (EC 132/2023)
Although Brazil's tax reform is being implemented gradually, its strategic direction is already clear.
The constitutional pillars have been approved, giving a high degree of certainty about the future
impact.
Transition phase: 2026
In 2026 a symbolic 1% test rate (0.9% CBS + 0.1% IBS) applies to all taxable operations, including
imports. This rate is not an additional cost: the importer can deduct it directly from PIS/COFINS due
in the same period. The goal is to force companies to update their invoicing systems (NFe 4.0/5.0)
— a kind of operational sandbox.
Main structural changes

End of ICMS-ST: tax is paid on actual sales, removing the financial risk of advance collection.

Reduced rate for food: with a standard rate of ~26.5% and a ~60% reduction for food, ajvar's
effective rate would be ~10–11%.

Digital tax credits: non-cumulativity becomes absolute — VAT paid on import generates an
immediate, transparent digital credit.

End of regional incentives: RioLog, MG Import Corridor, TTD 409 and FUNDAP will be phased out by
2032.

Split payment: VAT will be withheld automatically at the moment of the financial transaction,
requiring more robust working-capital management.
Strategically, the reform will make the Brazilian market healthier, more transparent and more
meritocratic. For premium, value-driven products like ajvar this change is fundamentally positive:
it levels the playing field, rewarding operators who invest in strong products and efficient
operations.

CHAPTER 11
Strategic Labelling and the 'Lupa'
In the Brazilian market, labelling is not a secondary or purely regulatory detail; it is a decisive
commercial factor. A label fully compliant with Brazilian rules, in Portuguese, is mandatory not
only to satisfy ANVISA but also to build consumer trust and protect the product's shelf positioning.
The 'Lupa': confirmation of compliance
ANVISA's front-of-pack warning system (RDC 429/2020), known as the 'Lupa' (magnifying glass),

strong negative visual signal — consumers do not read it as neutral information, but as a warning
associated with ultra-processed foods.
